# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway was a pioneering computer scientist and engineer who made groundbreaking contributions to Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) system design. Born in 1938 and raised as a boy who experienced gender dysphoria, she faced significant challenges, including being fired by IBM in 1968 after attempting to transition, a decision for which IBM later apologized in 2020. After completing her transition and adopting the name Lynn, she joined Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-authored the seminal textbook *Introduction to VLSI Systems* with Carver Mead. This work, sold over 70,000 copies by 1983, introduced scalable design rules and the Metal Oxide Semiconductor Implementation Service (MOSIS), revolutionizing how chips are designed and manufactured by enabling small companies and universities to access state-of-the-art fabrication.
Beyond her technical innovations, Conway is renowned for the "Mead-Conway VLSI design methodology," which laid the foundation for the modern foundry model and spurred the growth of the electronic design automation industry. She also coined the "Conway effect," describing the phenomenon where innovators who do not fit traditional societal expectations are overlooked in historical accounts. A prominent transgender rights activist, Conway advocated for legal protections and the de-pathologization of gender identity, serving as a "Stonewall 40 trans hero" and lobbying for LGBT inclusion in professional codes of ethics. Her legacy includes numerous awards, induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, and recognition as a revolutionary figure who bridged the gap between theoretical design and practical chip production.
